chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Early Global Crises (1929 to 1982)

body.text: Borrowing in dollars at a floating rate means your repayments are decided by someone else's central bank. In 1982, that someone was the US Federal Reserve, and Latin America could not pay.

children.text: In August 1982, Mexico's finance minister, Jesús Silva Herzog, delivered a message to the chairman of the US Federal Reserve, the US Treasury secretary and the head of the IMF. Mexico could no longer service its $80 billion of foreign debt. Within weeks, Mexico had nationalised its private banks. By October 1983, 16 other Latin American countries and 11 developing countries elsewhere had to reschedule their debts.

A decade earlier, lending to these governments had looked like the safest business in banking. This lesson explains how that belief was built, how it collapsed, and why the region called the years that followed "the lost decade".

children.text: Build-up: Petrodollars Looking for Borrowers

As you saw in the last lesson, the oil shocks left oil exporters with more dollars than they could spend. They parked those dollars in large Western banks, and the banks needed someone to lend them to. Latin American governments, which needed money to pay for expensive oil and ambitious development projects, were eager borrowers.
Most of this money was lent as
syndicated loans
, and almost all of it at floating rates tied to
LIBOR
. When LIBOR rose, the borrower's interest bill rose with it, automatically.

markDefs.definition: Large loans funded jointly by a group of banks, with one or more lead banks arranging the deal. They let banks share out the risk of lending very large sums to one borrower.

The London Interbank Offered Rate, a benchmark for what banks charged each other for short-term dollar loans. For decades, trillions of dollars of loans reset their interest rates off it. US dollar LIBOR has since been replaced by SOFR.

body.text: Bankers justified the lending with a now-infamous idea, attributed to Citibank chairman Walter Wriston: countries do not go bankrupt. His reasoning was that a country's land, people and resources never disappear. That is true, but it misses the point. A country can own enormous assets and still run out of the one thing its lenders want: dollars.

children.text: Trigger: Rates Up, Exports Down

To crush US inflation, the Volcker Fed pushed interest rates to levels not seen in modern times. The US prime lending rate hit a record 21.5% in December 1980. Every floating rate loan in Latin America repriced upwards. At the same moment, a global recession in 1981 cut demand and prices for the region's exports, so the dollars needed to pay those higher bills shrank.
The key measure lenders watch is the
debt service ratio

markDefs.definition: Annual payments of interest and principal on foreign debt, divided by annual export earnings. It shows how much of a country's foreign income is already committed to its lenders.

body.caption: Above roughly a third, a country has little room left to import essentials if anything goes wrong.
A hypothetical Latin American borrower, before and after the rate shock ($ billion)

body.title: Calculate the Crisis Ratio
body.prompt: Using the "After" column in the table above, what is the borrower's debt service ratio? Give your answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Debt service ratio = $11.5 billion ÷ $17 billion × 100 = 67.6%. Before the shock, about a third of export earnings went to lenders. After it, more than two thirds do, leaving too little to pay for oil, food and machinery. The country did not borrow a single extra dollar. Higher rates and weaker exports did all the damage.

events.title: The lending boom

events.title: Global recession

events.title: The Baker Plan
events.description: The US proposes new lending tied to economic reforms. It buys time, but the debts keep growing.

events.title: The Brady Plan
events.description: The US shifts from more lending to debt reduction. Banks accept losses in exchange for safer, tradable bonds.

events.title: Mexico's Brady deal
events.description: Mexico becomes the first country to restructure under the Brady Plan.

children.text: Remember the wake-up call channel from Chapter 1. Once Mexico stopped paying, lenders looked at every borrower with a similar profile: Brazil, Argentina, Venezuela and more. They refused to roll over maturing loans for the entire region at once, which forced country after country into the same corner.

body.title: Why Floating Rates Were the Fatal Detail
body.question: Two countries each borrowed $10 billion in 1978. Country A borrowed at a fixed 8% for ten years. Country B borrowed at LIBOR plus 1%, when LIBOR was 7%. What happened to their interest bills when US rates soared in 1980 and 1981?
options: Both bills rose, because all loans reprice when the Fed raises rates
Country A's bill stayed the same, while Country B's rose sharply
Country B's bill stayed the same, while Country A's rose sharply
Neither bill changed, because the loans were already signed
body.explanation: A fixed rate loan locks in the interest rate for its life, so Country A kept paying 8%. Country B's rate reset upwards every time LIBOR rose, so its bill ballooned without it borrowing another dollar. Most Latin American debt looked like Country B's, which is why US monetary policy became a Latin American crisis.

children.text: Policy Response: Saving the Banks Quietly

The crisis was not just a problem for borrowers. The nine largest US banks had lent Latin America amounts equal to 176% of their capital. If those loans had been written down to their real value, several of America's biggest banks would have been insolvent.
So regulators chose
regulatory forbearance

. Loans were rescheduled rather than written off, and banks were given years to build up capital and reserves. The IMF lent to the countries on condition of harsh austerity, and much of that money flowed straight back to the banks as interest.

markDefs.definition: A decision by regulators to temporarily relax the enforcement of rules, such as recognising losses, to give troubled banks time to rebuild capital instead of forcing them into insolvency.

body.text: Notice the echo of Chapter 1's evergreening lesson. Rescheduling loans that cannot realistically be repaid keeps them looking alive on a bank's books. It can buy valuable time, but the loss does not vanish. Someone eventually absorbs it, and in the 1980s it was mainly the people of Latin America.

body.title: Go deeper: how Brady bonds finally broke the deadlock

children.text: By 1989, it was clear the debts would never be repaid in full, and seven years of rescheduling had not changed that. US Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady proposed a new approach: accept a loss, but make what remains safer and tradable.
Banks swapped their old loans for new 30-year bonds, called Brady bonds.
In Mexico's deal, banks could take bonds at a 35% discount to the face value of their loans, or keep full face value at a below-market fixed rate of 6.25%.
The principal of the new bonds was backed by US Treasury zero-coupon bonds, so investors knew they would get it back at maturity.
Because the bonds traded in markets, banks could sell them and move on, and new investors could take their place.

Example: a bank holding a $10 billion loan to Mexico that chose the discount option received $6.5 billion of Brady bonds. It booked a $3.5 billion loss, but held a safer asset it could actually sell. Debt relief plus credible collateral is what finally ended the crisis.

body.title: Name the Aftermath
body.textWithBlank: Because of the years of weak growth that followed the 1982 debt crisis, Latin Americans call the 1980s the lost ___.
body.explanation: The lost decade. Much of the region spent the 1980s cutting imports and investment to keep paying foreign lenders, and incomes stagnated or fell until debt relief arrived at the end of the decade.

children.text: India's Different Path in the 1980s

India escaped the 1982 crisis largely because it had borrowed far less from Western commercial banks in the 1970s. After the second oil shock squeezed its balance of payments, it went to the IMF instead.

body.label: India's Precautionary IMF Loan
body.context: At the time, it was the largest arrangement in IMF history. India drew only SDR 3.9 billion and asked to cancel the rest in 1984, once its position had improved.

children.text: But the story does not end there. In the second half of the 1980s, India began borrowing more from commercial lenders and relying on deposits from non-resident Indians, which can leave quickly. The warning signs from Latin America were visible, and India would face its own version in 1991. That is where Chapter 3 begins.

body.title: A 1982 Lesson for an Indian Company Today
body.scenario: An Indian infrastructure company earns all its revenue in rupees. It borrows $100 million through an external commercial borrowing (ECB) at a floating rate linked to SOFR, and does not hedge. At the start, its all-in interest rate is 5.5% and the rupee is at ₹83 per dollar. Two years later, US rates have risen so the loan costs 8.5%, and the rupee has weakened to ₹90.
body.prompt: Calculate the company's annual interest bill in rupees at the start and after two years, and explain which lessons from the 1982 crisis apply.
body.modelAnswer: At the start: $100 million × 5.5% = $5.5 million a year. At ₹83, that is ₹45.65 crore. After two years: $100 million × 8.5% = $8.5 million. At ₹90, that is ₹76.5 crore. The rupee interest bill has risen by about 68%, and the company has not borrowed any more. Three lessons from 1982 apply. First, floating rate debt hands control of your costs to a foreign central bank, just as Latin America's LIBOR loans did. Second, currency mismatch: the company earns rupees but owes dollars, so a weaker rupee raises its costs on top of higher rates, the same double squeeze countries faced when their currencies fell. Third, the debt service ratio matters more than the size of the debt: if the company's rupee cash flow has not grown by 68%, a larger share of its earnings now goes to lenders, and lenders will notice. This is why the RBI's ECB rules, and careful investors, pay close attention to hedging and to whether a borrower has natural dollar income.

body.title: The 1982 Red Flag Checklist, for Countries or Companies
steps: Is a large share of the debt in a foreign currency, while income is in the local currency?
Is most of the debt at floating rates that reset with foreign interest rates?
Is the debt service ratio above roughly a third of foreign earnings?
Does the borrower depend on a few commodity exports or a single customer for its foreign income?
Is a lot of debt maturing soon, so it needs lenders to keep rolling it over?
Is the borrower claiming it cannot fail because its assets are large, even though they cannot easily be turned into cash?

points: Petrodollars recycled by Western banks drove Latin American external debt from $75 billion in 1975 to over $315 billion by 1983
Floating rate dollar loans meant the Volcker Fed's rate hikes, including a 21.5% US prime rate, flowed straight into borrowers' interest bills
Mexico's announcement in August 1982 triggered a regional crisis, and 27 developing countries had rescheduled by October 1983
Regulators protected overexposed US banks through forbearance, while Latin America suffered a lost decade until the 1989 Brady Plan cut the debt
India avoided the 1982 crisis with a precautionary IMF loan, but its later build-up of commercial and NRI borrowing set up its own crisis in 1991
